AbstractText.Label: STUDY DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Prospective cohort study OBJECTIVE.: To identify potential prognostic factors for persistent leg-pain at 12 months amongst patients hospitalised with acute severe sciatica.

AbstractText.Label: SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND DATA
AbstractText.content: The long-term outcome for patients admitted to hospital with sciatica is generally unfavourable. Results concerning prognostic factors for persistent sciatica are limited and conflicting.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: A total of 210 patients acutely admitted to hospital for either surgical or non-surgical treatment of sciatica were consecutively recruited and received a thorough clinical and radiographic examination in addition to responding to a comprehensive questionnaire. Follow-up assessments were done at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months. Potential prognostic factors were measured at baseline and at 6 weeks. The impact of these factors on leg-pain was analysed by multiple linear regression modelling.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 151 patients completed the entire study, 93 receiving non-randomised surgical treatment. The final multivariate models showed that the following factors were significantly associated with leg-pain at 12-months; high psychosocial risk according to the Örebro Musculosceletal Pain Questionnaire (unstandardized beta coefficient 1.55, 95% confidence interval 0.72-2.38, p < 0.001), not receiving surgical treatment (1.11, 0.29-1.93, p = 0.01), not actively employed upon admission (1.47, 0.63-2.31, p < 0.01), and self-reported leg-pain recorded 6 weeks post hospital admission (0.49, 0.34-0.63, p < 0.001). Interaction analysis showed that the Örebro Musculosceletal Pain Questionnaire had significant prognostic value only on the non-surgically treated patients (3.26, 1.89-4.63, p < 0.001).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The results suggest that a psychosocial screening tool and the implementation of a 6-week post admission follow-up has prognostic value in the hospital management of severe sciatica.
